subject: biology
title: BIO1011 practice exam
summary: A full timed practice exam for BIO1011 with six short-answer questions and worked solutions, plus 20 exam-style multiple-choice questions covering cells, molecules, enzymes, energy, division and genetics.
body:
This practice exam covers the whole of BIO1011 at the level of a first-year university final exam. It tests recall, but mostly it tests whether you can apply ideas to data and unfamiliar scenarios. Treat it like the real thing, then mark yourself honestly against the worked solutions.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 2 hours in total. Allow about 40 minutes for the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 80 minutes for the short-answer section (roughly 1.5 minutes per mark).
- **Conditions:** closed book, no notes. A basic calculator is allowed. Work in a quiet place without your phone.
- **Order:** do the short-answer questions first on paper, under timed conditions, before you open the worked solutions. Then do the multiple-choice questions below.
- **Marking:** the short-answer section is worth 40 marks. Give yourself a mark only when your answer contains the point named in the solution. Write down every topic where you lost marks and go back to that lesson.
- **Command words:** "describe" means say what happens; "explain" means say what happens and why; "calculate" means show the formula, substitution, working and units.

## Topics covered

- Cell structure, endosymbiosis and microscopy calculations
- Biological molecules and condensation and hydrolysis
- Metabolism, free energy, ATP coupling and enzyme kinetics (Km, Vmax, inhibition)
- Cellular respiration (including inhibitor experiments) and photosynthesis
- Tissues, differentiation and stem cells
- The cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis and non-disjunction
- Molecular genetics: replication, transcription, translation, the lac operon and mutation
- Mendelian genetics: crosses, chi-square, linkage and sex linkage
- Apoptosis, necrosis, telomeres, senescence and cancer

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (6 marks)

A cell biologist follows a radioactively labelled amino acid through a pancreatic cell that secretes digestive enzymes. Radioactivity is detected first in one organelle, then in a second, then in vesicles, and finally outside the cell.

(a) Name, in order, the two organelles where the label appears first and second, and state what happens to the protein in each. (4 marks)

(b) Explain why a protein that will be secreted is made on a ribosome attached to the ER rather than a free ribosome. (2 marks)

### Question 2 (7 marks)

An enzyme was assayed with and without compound X. The results were:

| Condition | Vmax (µmol min⁻¹) | Km (mM) |
|---|---|---|
| No inhibitor | 150 | 3.0 |
| + compound X | 75 | 3.0 |

(a) Calculate the initial rate without the inhibitor when [S] = 6.0 mM. Show your working. (2 marks)

(b) Calculate the initial rate with compound X at the same [S]. (1 mark)

(c) Identify the type of inhibition shown by X and explain how the data support your answer. (2 marks)

(d) Explain whether adding much more substrate would restore the original maximum rate. (2 marks)

### Question 3 (7 marks)

Mitochondria are isolated and placed in a buffer containing pyruvate, ADP and Pᵢ. Oxygen use is measured as substances are added.

(a) Explain why oxygen use stops completely when cyanide (a Complex IV inhibitor) is added. (2 marks)

(b) In a fresh sample, oligomycin (which blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase) is added. ATP synthesis stops and oxygen use falls sharply. Explain why oxygen use falls even though the electron transport chain itself is not blocked. (3 marks)

(c) The drug DNP is then added to the oligomycin-treated sample, and oxygen use rises sharply again, but no ATP is made. Explain these results. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (6 marks)

A species has 2n = 6.

(a) Complete the following for one cell: number of chromosomes and DNA content (taking a G1 cell as 2c) at (i) G2, (ii) the end of meiosis I (one cell), (iii) the end of meiosis II (one cell). (3 marks)

(b) In a human, the sex chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis I of a father's sperm-producing cell. State the sex chromosome content of the four sperm produced, and name one possible condition in a child produced from one of them fertilising a normal egg. (3 marks)

### Question 5 (8 marks)

In a plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p) and tall stems (T) are dominant to short (t). A plant heterozygous for both genes is test-crossed with a pp tt plant. The 400 offspring are:

| Phenotype | Number |
|---|---|
| Purple tall | 168 |
| Purple short | 34 |
| White tall | 32 |
| White short | 166 |

(a) State the expected numbers if the genes assort independently, and state the null hypothesis. (2 marks)

(b) Calculate χ² and state your conclusion. The critical value for df = 3 at p = 0.05 is 7.81. (4 marks)

(c) Calculate the recombination frequency and the map distance between the two genes. (2 marks)

### Question 6 (6 marks)

Normal human fibroblasts stop dividing after a limited number of divisions in culture, but cancer cells taken from a tumour keep dividing indefinitely.

(a) Explain why telomeres shorten each time a normal cell divides. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why cancer cells can keep dividing indefinitely. (2 marks)

(c) Cancer cells also often carry a mutated *TP53* gene. Explain how loss of p53 function helps a cancer cell survive. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Solution 1

(a)
- First: **rough endoplasmic reticulum** (1 mark). The protein is made by ribosomes on the rough ER and threaded into the ER lumen, where it folds and may have sugars added (glycosylation) (1 mark).
- Second: **Golgi apparatus** (1 mark). The protein is further modified (for example, sugar chains trimmed or added), sorted and packaged into secretory vesicles (1 mark).

(b) The start of the polypeptide carries a **signal sequence** that is recognised as it emerges, which directs the ribosome to the ER membrane (1 mark). The protein is fed into the ER lumen and so enters the endomembrane route that ends in exocytosis; a protein made on a free ribosome stays in the cytosol and cannot be secreted (1 mark).

### Solution 2

(a) Formula: v₀ = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]) (1 mark). v₀ = 150 × 6.0 ÷ (3.0 + 6.0) = 900 ÷ 9.0 = **100 µmol min⁻¹** (1 mark).

(b) v₀ = 75 × 6.0 ÷ 9.0 = 450 ÷ 9.0 = **50 µmol min⁻¹** (1 mark).

(c) **Non-competitive inhibition** (1 mark). Vmax is halved but Km is unchanged, so X does not compete for the active site; it reduces the number of working enzyme molecules (or their catalytic rate), while those still active bind substrate as well as before (1 mark).

(d) No (1 mark). X binds somewhere other than the active site, so extra substrate cannot displace it; the maximum rate stays at 75 µmol min⁻¹ however much substrate is added (1 mark).

### Solution 3

(a) Cyanide stops electrons passing from Complex IV to oxygen, so oxygen is no longer reduced to water (1 mark). Electrons back up along the whole chain, so no electron transport (and no oxygen use) can occur (1 mark).

(b) With ATP synthase blocked, H⁺ cannot flow back into the matrix (1 mark). The chain keeps pumping H⁺ out until the gradient becomes very steep, and pumping against this gradient takes more energy than electron transport can supply (1 mark). Electron transport therefore slows, so less oxygen is used. This shows that electron transport and ATP synthesis are **coupled** (1 mark).

(c) DNP is an **uncoupler**: it carries H⁺ across the inner membrane, bypassing ATP synthase (1 mark). The gradient collapses, so electron transport and oxygen use run quickly again, but because ATP synthase is still blocked and the gradient is dissipated, no ATP is made; the energy is released as heat (1 mark).

### Solution 4

(a) (1 mark each)
- (i) G2: **6 chromosomes, 4c** (each chromosome has two chromatids).
- (ii) End of meiosis I: **3 chromosomes, 2c** (haploid, but chromatids still joined).
- (iii) End of meiosis II: **3 chromosomes, 1c**.

(b) Non-disjunction in meiosis I puts both X and Y in one secondary cell and no sex chromosome in the other (1 mark). After a normal meiosis II, two sperm are **XY** and two have **no sex chromosome (O)** (1 mark). An XY sperm fertilising an X egg gives XXY (**Klinefelter syndrome**); an O sperm fertilising an X egg gives XO (**Turner syndrome**). Either earns the mark (1 mark).

### Solution 5

(a) Independent assortment predicts a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio, so **100 of each** class (1 mark). H₀: the two genes assort independently and any difference between observed and expected numbers is due to chance (1 mark).

(b)

| Phenotype | O | E | (O − E)² ÷ E |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purple tall | 168 | 100 | 68² ÷ 100 = 46.24 |
| Purple short | 34 | 100 | 66² ÷ 100 = 43.56 |
| White tall | 32 | 100 | 68² ÷ 100 = 46.24 |
| White short | 166 | 100 | 66² ÷ 100 = 43.56 |
| **Total** | 400 | 400 | **χ² = 179.6** |

- Correct method and table (1 mark); χ² = 179.6 (1 mark).
- df = 4 − 1 = 3; 179.6 is far greater than 7.81, so p is less than 0.05 (1 mark).
- Reject H₀: the genes do not assort independently; they are **linked** (1 mark).

(c) Parental classes are the two largest: purple tall and white short, so the heterozygote was PT/pt. Recombinants = 34 + 32 = 66. RF = 66 ÷ 400 × 100% = **16.5%** (1 mark). Map distance = **16.5 map units (cM)** (1 mark).

### Solution 6

(a) DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end, so the lagging strand needs an RNA primer (1 mark). At the very end of the chromosome the last primer is removed and the gap cannot be filled, so each round of replication leaves the new strand slightly shorter: the **end-replication problem** (1 mark).

(b) Most cancer cells switch on **telomerase**, a reverse transcriptase that uses its own RNA template to add telomere repeats (1 mark). Telomere length is therefore maintained, so the cells never reach the critically short length that triggers senescence and the Hayflick limit does not apply (1 mark).

(c) p53 is a **tumour suppressor** that responds to DNA damage by halting the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint to allow repair (1 mark) and, if damage is too severe, by triggering **apoptosis** (for example by promoting pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins). Without p53, damaged cells neither stop nor die, so they keep dividing and accumulate more mutations (1 mark).

questions.prompt: An unknown cell is 3 µm long, has 70S ribosomes, no nucleus and a cell wall without peptidoglycan. What is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: No nucleus and 70S ribosomes mean a prokaryote. Bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan, so a prokaryote without it is most likely an archaeon. A is tempting because bacteria are the more familiar prokaryotes, but the missing peptidoglycan rules them out. Yeast and plant cells are eukaryotes with nuclei and 80S ribosomes.

questions.prompt: A scale bar labelled 5 µm measures 20 mm on a micrograph. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Convert to the same units: 20 mm = 20 000 µm. Magnification = 20 000 ÷ 5 = ×4000. ×4 comes from dividing 20 by 5 without converting units, the most common error.

questions.prompt: Which statement about microtubules is correct?

options.A: They form the cleavage furrow that pinches an animal cell in two
options.B: They are made of actin and interact with myosin in muscle
options.C: They form the mitotic spindle and act as tracks for kinesin and dynein
options.D: They are the main fibres giving the nuclear envelope its strength

questions.explanation: Microtubules (made of tubulin) form the spindle and are the tracks that kinesin and dynein walk along. A and B describe actin microfilaments, which form the contractile ring in cytokinesis and work with myosin. The nuclear lamina is made of intermediate filaments.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 31% guanine. What percentage is thymine?
questions.explanation: G = C = 31%, so G + C = 62%. A + T = 38%, and A = T, so T = 19%. 38% is the combined A + T figure, a common slip from forgetting to halve it.

questions.prompt: Heating a protein to 90 °C causes it to lose its function. Which bonds are NOT broken during this denaturation?
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the weaker interactions that hold secondary and tertiary structure (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions), so the shape is lost. Peptide bonds are covalent and stay intact, so the primary structure is unchanged. Hydrogen bonds (A) are the bonds most easily broken by heat.

questions.prompt: Reaction X has ΔG°′ = +21 kJ mol⁻¹. It is coupled to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹). What is ΔG°′ for the coupled reaction, and does it proceed?

options.A: +51.5 kJ mol⁻¹; it does not proceed
options.C: +9.5 kJ mol⁻¹; it does not proceed

questions.explanation: Add the ΔG values: +21 + (−30.5) = −9.5 kJ mol⁻¹. A negative ΔG means the coupled reaction is exergonic and can proceed. C has the right size but the wrong sign; D subtracts instead of adding.

questions.prompt: Hexokinase has a Km for glucose of about 0.1 mM and glucokinase has a Km of about 10 mM. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Glucokinase has the higher affinity for glucose
options.B: Glucokinase always works faster than hexokinase
options.C: Both enzymes are saturated at a blood glucose of 5 mM
options.D: Hexokinase reaches half its Vmax at a much lower glucose concentration

questions.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax, so hexokinase (Km 0.1 mM) reaches half speed at a much lower glucose level and has the higher affinity. A reverses the meaning of Km: a high Km means low affinity. At 5 mM, glucokinase is still well below saturation, so C is wrong.

questions.prompt: End product Z of a pathway binds to a site away from the active site of the first enzyme and switches it off. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: An end product binding a regulatory site (not the active site) on an early enzyme is allosteric feedback inhibition, which stops the cell making more Z than it needs. It is not competitive inhibition because Z does not bind the active site, and it is reversible as Z levels fall.

questions.prompt: Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, how much ATP is produced from the NADH and FADH₂ formed in the citric acid cycle alone, per glucose?
questions.explanation: Per glucose, the citric acid cycle (two turns) produces 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂. 6 × 2.5 = 15 and 2 × 1.5 = 3, giving 18 ATP. 15 counts only the NADH; 25 counts all 10 NADH from the whole of respiration.

questions.prompt: Yeast cells are moved from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Which change is expected?

options.A: Glucose use per minute falls because less ATP is needed
options.B: The citric acid cycle continues but the electron transport chain stops
options.C: Ethanol and CO₂ are produced, and NAD⁺ is regenerated so glycolysis can continue
options.D: Lactate is produced to regenerate FAD

questions.explanation: Without oxygen, yeast ferments pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂, which reoxidises NADH to NAD⁺ so glycolysis keeps making 2 ATP per glucose. Glucose use actually rises because each glucose gives far less ATP. Lactate fermentation occurs in animals, not yeast, and regenerates NAD⁺, not FAD.

questions.prompt: In the light-dependent reactions, where are H⁺ ions most concentrated?

options.C: In the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion

questions.explanation: Photolysis releases H⁺ inside the thylakoid and the electron transport chain pumps more in, so the lumen has the highest H⁺ concentration. H⁺ flows out through ATP synthase into the stroma, where ATP is made. C is the equivalent site in mitochondria, a common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Which pair of features best identifies tissue as xylem?

options.A: Living sieve tube elements with companion cells
options.B: Dividing, undifferentiated cells at the tip of a root
options.C: Living cells with unevenly thickened walls that support young stems
options.D: Dead, hollow cells with lignified walls that carry water

questions.explanation: Xylem vessels and tracheids are dead at maturity, hollow and strengthened with lignin, and carry water and minerals. A describes phloem, B describes an apical meristem and C describes collenchyma.

questions.prompt: Skin cells and liver cells from the same person differ in function. What is the main reason?

options.A: Each cell type has lost the genes it does not need
options.B: They express different sets of genes from the same genome
options.C: They contain different numbers of chromosomes

questions.explanation: Differentiated cells keep the full genome but switch different genes on and off using transcription factors and epigenetic marks. A is the classic misconception; cloning and iPSC experiments show that differentiated cells still have all their genes.

questions.prompt: A drug that prevents microtubules from assembling is added to dividing cells. At which stage do cells become arrested, and why?

options.A: G1, because the G1 checkpoint detects DNA damage
options.B: S phase, because DNA polymerase needs microtubules
options.C: Metaphase, because the spindle checkpoint detects unattached kinetochores
options.D: Cytokinesis, because the cleavage furrow cannot form

questions.explanation: Without microtubules no spindle can form, so kinetochores remain unattached and the spindle checkpoint stops cells entering anaphase. Cells pile up with condensed chromosomes and 4c DNA. D is tempting, but the cleavage furrow is made of actin, and cells never get that far.

questions.prompt: Which event in meiosis directly produces new combinations of alleles on a single chromosome?

options.A: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I
options.C: Separation of sister chromatids at anaphase II

questions.explanation: Crossing over swaps segments between non-sister chromatids of homologues, creating chromosomes with new combinations of alleles. Independent assortment (B) produces new combinations of whole chromosomes, not new combinations within one chromosome.

questions.prompt: Why are Okazaki fragments formed on only one strand during DNA replication?

options.A: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so one strand must be made in short pieces away from the fork
options.B: Helicase unwinds only one strand at a time
options.C: Primase can only bind to the leading strand
options.D: Ligase joins the leading strand into pieces after replication

questions.explanation: The two strands are antiparallel and DNA polymerase only works 5′ → 3′. The leading strand can be made continuously towards the fork, but the lagging strand must be made backwards in short Okazaki fragments, each needing a primer. C is wrong because primase is needed many times on the lagging strand.

questions.prompt: A deletion of three consecutive bases from the coding region of a gene would most likely:

options.A: Change every amino acid after the deletion
options.B: Have no effect because the reading frame is maintained
options.C: Remove one amino acid but keep the rest of the reading frame
options.D: Always produce a premature stop codon

questions.explanation: Deleting three bases removes one codon, so the reading frame after the deletion is unchanged and one amino acid is lost (sometimes two codons are affected, changing one amino acid). A describes a frameshift, which happens when the number of bases is not a multiple of three. B is wrong because losing an amino acid can still change the protein.

questions.prompt: A man with an X-linked recessive disorder has children with a woman who is homozygous normal. What proportion of their daughters will be carriers?
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives her father's only X chromosome, which carries the recessive allele, and a normal X from her mother, so all daughters are carriers. Sons receive their father's Y, so none are affected. 50% is the answer for daughters of a carrier mother and normal father.

questions.prompt: Crossing two white-flowered sweet pea plants gives an F₁ of all purple flowers; the F₂ ratio is 9 purple : 7 white. What best explains this?

options.B: Two genes are linked, so recombinants are rare
options.C: A single gene with a lethal allele
options.D: Epistasis: purple needs a dominant allele at both of two genes

questions.explanation: A 9 : 7 ratio is a modified 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, showing two genes. Only plants with at least one dominant allele at both genes (the 9) make purple; the other 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 are white. Linked genes (B) would not give a clean ratio based on sixteenths, and a single gene cannot give a 16-part ratio.

questions.prompt: In the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, which event directly leads to activation of caspase-9?

options.A: A death ligand binding to Fas on the cell surface
options.B: Cytochrome c released from mitochondria binding Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome
options.C: Telomerase adding repeats to chromosome ends

questions.explanation: In the intrinsic pathway, Bcl-2 family proteins allow cytochrome c to leave the mitochondria; it binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9 and the caspase cascade. A starts the extrinsic pathway, which activates caspase-8 first. D describes necrosis.
